latin: Bene prandisti? — Ita, mihi prandio apposita sunt<sup>1</sup>:

Promulsis<sup>2</sup> varia, praecipue artocreas<sup>3</sup> suillum, bis duodenae cochleae<sup>4</sup>, gallus in vino coctus<sup>5</sup> cum cepulis<sup>6</sup>, haec omnia mero burgundico large perfusa<sup>7</sup>.
Nonne cerritus es? Jam mihi dixisti te stomacho laborare. Pinguior<sup>8</sup> es, vultus tuus purpura tinctus<sup>9</sup> videtur, nasus papulis gemmat<sup>10</sup>. Num ver appropinquat?
Num tu te facetum esse arbitraris?
Tantum tibi dicam, rectius te, istorum ciborum plumbeorum<sup>11</sup> loco, comesturum fuisse assulam bubulam<sup>12</sup> cum solanis frictis<sup>13</sup>.
Nihil timueris, vetus amice, postea enim assulam bubulam cum solanis frictis habui.
In aedibus urbanissimis, aes<sup>14</sup> telephonii tinnit<sup>15</sup>.
Nestor, famulus cubicularius, cum ea dignitate quam in omnibus actis domesticis adhibere<sup>16</sup> solet, instrumentum capit.
Vox in telephonio. — Salve funge! Esne tu, vetule<sup>17</sup> asine?
Nestor, aucta etiam dignitate. — Veniam mihi da, Domne, ego sum Nestor, cubicularius. Erus<sup>18</sup> autem abest!
english: Did you lunch well? — Yes, [I had] for lunch (to me for lunch have been served):
Assorted hors d'oeuvres, especially pork pâté, [two dozen] (twice twelve) snails, coq au vin with small onions, all of it washed down generously with [Burgundy] (pure) wine.

Aren't you [crazy] (furious)? You have already told me that [you had stomach trouble] (you to work by stomach). You are too fat, your face looks dyed with purple, [your] nose is budding with pimples. Is spring approaching, by any chance?
Do you think by any chance [that you are being] funny?
I'll just tell you that [you would have done better] (more rightly you) to eat, instead of those [heavy dishes] (leaden foods), a [steak] (beef slice) with chips.
Don't worry (subj. pft) about anything, [my] old [friend], after that I did in fact [have] a steak and chips.
In a very bourgeois house, the telephone bell rings.
Nestor, the valet, with the dignity which he is in the habit of showing in all his domestic acts, picks up the [receiver] (instrument).
The voice on the telephone. — Hello, [idiot] (mushroom)! Is it you, old donkey?
Nestor, [with even more dignity] (increased still dignity). — Excuse me, sir, [this is] (I am) Nestor, the valet. Sir is not here!

footnotes: Mihi prandio apposita sunt: another double dative! Apponere = ad + ponere, to bring, to serve.
Promulsis, promulsidis, f., the hors d'oeuvre; word of Greek origin (used in the singular).
Artocreas, -atis, n., another word of Greek origin («artos», bread; «kreas», meat).
Cochlea, -ae, f., the snail, an important word, for it serves by extension to give the idea of a coiled curve, and consequently designates the screw.
Cepa, -ae, f., onion; cepula is its diminutive (which gave in Italian «cipolla» onion... and in French ciboule, ciboulette, ciboulot). The cep or boletus (mushroom) is called boletus.
Perfundo, -is, -ere, fudi, fusum, derived from fundere, to pour, which you will find in the exercise, phrase 7.
Pinguis, -e, fat; pinguior, -ius is its comparative.
Purpura, -ae, f., the red dye, obtained from a shellfish, the murex, -icis, m. Tingo, -is, -ere, tinxi, tinctum, to dye.
Gemma, -ae, f., bud, flower bud, precious stone; whence the verb gemmare, to bud. Papula designates another sort of button, those that sometimes flourish on human skin.
Plumbum, -i, n., lead; plumbeus, -a, -um, of lead. Likewise ferrum, iron, gives ferreus; etc. An iron box, pyxis ferrea (or e ferro).
Assula, -ae, a slice. The English word «beefsteak» means precisely beef slice. Likewise (in the exercise) «cocktail» means cock's tail, whence the Latin gallicauda.
Solanum, -i, n., the potato, which belongs to the solanaceae family. Frigo, -is, -ere, frixi, frictum, to fry.
Aes, aeris, n., bronze, and, by extension, the instrument of music (cf. French cuivre, brass), the bell. The corresponding adjective is aereus, or aeneus (cf. E. 64, P. 5).
Tinnire, to tinkle, gave tintinnabulum, the bell, a word that could very well have been used instead of aes.
Adhibere = ad habere, to apply, to put into practice, to have recourse to, is a verb with multiple uses.
Erus, -i, m., the master of the house; f. era, -ae.
comments: Propoma, -atis, n., aperitif (synonyms: potio apertiva or vinum apertivum). — Idoneus, -a, -um, appropriate to, gave French idoine. — Uva, -ae, f., grape; vitis, -is, f., the vine; vinea, -ae, f., the vineyard, the arbour or the mantlet (war machine serving as a shelter). — Note the two subjunctives of phrase 5 (indirect question) and also necne which, in an indirect question, corresponds to annon of the direct question.

latin: Quota hora est?
Undecima et dimidia hora est.
Nondum tempus est prandendi. Sed quid arbitraris* de quodam propomate sumendo?
Omnis occasio ad bibendum tibi idonea videtur.
Non a te quaero utrum avia tua birota utatur necne, sed quid bibere velis*: anisum, absinthium, merum, an gallicaudam?
Malo* aurantii aut uvae sucum.
Ecce! Aurantium premo ejusque sucum in poculum fundo. Visne* saccharum?
Ita: da cubos duos. Potionem cochleari agito.
Prosit*! — Bene tibi! — Bene tibi quoque!
Quid olfacio? Optime olet! Hic odor e culina venit.
Pullus gallinaceus in culina coquitur: odorem pulli olfacimus.
Eamus pransum!
english: What time is it?
It's half past eleven.
It's not yet time to have lunch. But what do you think of a (certain) aperitif (to take)?
Every opportunity to drink seems good to you.
I'm not asking you whether your grandmother [rides] (uses) a bicycle or not, but what you want to drink: anise, absinthe, wine or a cocktail?
I would prefer orange or grape juice.
Here you are! I squeeze the orange, and I pour its juice into a glass. Do you want sugar?
Yes, give [me] two [lumps] (cubes). I stir the drink with a spoon.
Your health! — To yours! — To yours too!
What do I smell? That smells very good. This smell comes from the kitchen.
A chicken (gallinaceous) is cooking in the kitchen: we [can smell] the chicken.
Let's go and have lunch!
